name: MMS (chlorine dioxide)

lead: MMS is the name given to a chlorine dioxide solution made by mixing sodium chlorite with an acid. Its promoters have described it as a cure for dozens of conditions, and acne is the skin condition most often named, which is how it entered conversations about clearer skin.

No clinical trial has shown it clears skin or treats the other conditions claimed for it. Regulators in many countries have issued warnings about drinking it, and chlorine dioxide is otherwise known as an industrial bleaching and disinfecting agent.

paras: Promoters have described taking it by mouth after activating the solution with an acid such as citrus juice or vinegar, and some variants are sold as CDS or used as baths or enemas. Sellers sometimes label it a water purifier. Followers often describe nausea, vomiting and diarrhea as a sign it is working. This wiki does not give preparation or amounts.

Health agencies report nausea, vomiting, diarrhea and dangerously low blood pressure from dehydration; sodium chlorite can cause kidney failure and, in people with G6PD deficiency, life-threatening blood reactions. The FDA has told consumers to stop using and dispose of it. Several sellers have been prosecuted in the US, Canada and elsewhere.

angle.text: Promoters list acne among the conditions the solution is said to resolve, and some users take it hoping for clearer skin. Regulators document gastrointestinal, circulatory and kidney harms from ingestion, and no trial has measured a skin benefit.

lead: MMS, short for Miracle Mineral Solution or Supplement, is an aqueous chlorine dioxide preparation created by mixing sodium chlorite with an acid. The name was coined by Jim Humble in his self-published 2006 book The Miracle Mineral Solution of the 21st Century [1]. Variants are sold as CDS or the CD protocol [1].

In appearance and skin-care discussion, MMS appears because Humble's list of claimed uses included acne, the only specific skin condition in the claims, alongside illnesses such as malaria, HIV and cancer [1]. Believers who take it therefore sometimes describe it as a way to clear skin from the inside, with detox as the claimed route to clearer skin.

No clinical trials support the claims made for it [1]. Health agencies in Belgium, France, Canada, the UK, Australia and the United States have issued warnings about its toxicity, and the US FDA has likened drinking it to drinking bleach [1]. Chlorine dioxide itself is a well-characterised industrial oxidizer used for bleaching and water treatment [2].

paras: Chlorine dioxide is a yellow-green gas at room temperature that dissolves in water and is a strong, selective oxidizing agent used industrially for bleaching and disinfection [2]. MMS is made by activating sodium chlorite with an acid so that chlorine dioxide forms in solution [1]. Sellers have sometimes marketed it as a water purifier, which Wikipedia notes is a way to avoid medical regulation [1].

Jim Humble, a former Scientologist, introduced the name in 2006 [1]. The Genesis II Church of Health and Healing and affiliated groups promoted it in many countries, and during the COVID-19 pandemic they promoted it as a cure [1]. A 2020 forum thread on T Nation discussed news coverage of a leader of such a group writing to the US president about chlorine dioxide [3]. Humble said in 2016 that MMS cures nothing [1].

Humble claimed MMS cures HIV, malaria, hepatitis, influenza, colds, autism, acne and cancer [1]. For appearance, the relevant claim is acne. Followers describe vomiting and diarrhea after taking it as evidence it is clearing the body, a reading regulators dispute because those effects reflect toxicity [1].

Chlorine dioxide ingestion can cause nausea, vomiting, diarrhea and dangerously low blood pressure from dehydration [1]. Sodium chlorite can cause kidney failure at high amounts, intestinal inflammation at lower ones, and life-threatening reactions in people with G6PD deficiency [1]. The US EPA has noted that chronic exposure to small amounts may cause reproductive and neurodevelopmental harm [1].

Warnings have been issued by Belgium (2009), France (2010), Canada (2010 and 2012), the UK Food Standards Agency, and the FDA in 2010 and 2019 [1]. A woman died in Vanuatu in 2009 after taking MMS for malaria prevention, and a five-year-old boy died in Argentina in 2020 [1]. Concentrated chlorine dioxide is also explosive and is never stored in bulk industrially [2].

Louis Daniel Smith was sentenced in 2015 to over four years for smuggling and fraud, and Stanley Nowak was sentenced in British Columbia in 2018 [1]. In Florida a 2020 federal injunction stopped sales, and Mark and Joseph Grenon received 60-month sentences in 2023 [1]. Australia's TGA fined MMS Australia A$151,000 in 2020 [1].
No studies found. No clinical trial has tested MMS for acne or any other skin condition, and Wikipedia reports that claims for it rest on anecdote and Humble's book [1].

lore.intro: MMS circulates in health-fringe communities as a detox remedy; it appears only in passing on bodybuilding forums such as T Nation, usually in connection with news coverage [3].
